titulo: An afternoon doing what they do
subtitulo: Market, corner bar, square and the week the street belongs to everyone — how each one is entered, and why the rule that decides the rest is written by the town hall two streets away and not by Spain
cena: Ten past six on a Thursday, two streets up from the sand, your shirt still in your hand, and the square in front of you filling up with people who live here.
decisao: how the six hours between lunch and dinner get spent, and what the same six hours cost two hundred kilometres away — the shirt in your hand, the can in the street and the blanket you buy the bag off are each priced by the town hall you happen to be standing in, and the amounts run from a hundred to six hundred euros, taken on the spot in Barcelona since February

clique.desconto: Nobody handed you those sentences. You owned the frame already, and the afternoon only changed what went in it.
clique.piso: You will spend a Spanish afternoon where they spend it, and pay what they pay for it. Most visitors spend a fortnight within sight of the seafront.

frasePiso: You will spend a Spanish afternoon where they spend it, and pay what they pay for it. Most visitors spend a fortnight within sight of the seafront.
permissao: You are allowed to walk a whole market and buy nothing. You are allowed to make one small drink last a whole half at the bar, and one order hold a table in the square for an hour — that is what the order was for. You are allowed to stand in the middle of somebody else's street party: nobody at either end is checking a ticket, because there isn't one. And the can that is a problem in your hand is nothing at all on the terrace table two metres away.
espelho: Ordering a second one every twenty minutes to justify the chair is the bit that reads as odd there. Nobody is counting what is in front of you, and buying your way through the hour is the one thing that marks the table out.

fichasCulturais.sinal: Twenty past one on a Tuesday and the man at the stall has started stacking crates while you are still deciding.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: He has had enough of me, or the place is shutting early today and nobody said so.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: The small trade works two shifts and not one — roughly ten to half one, then again from about five until eight. The middle of the day is the gap between them, and the market is the first thing to go into it.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Do the market before half one or after five, and put whatever you meant to do in between at a table with a plate in front of you.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You get the market with the neighbourhood still in it instead of the tail end of it, and the empty hour turns into the long lunch it was always going to be.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not the big chains — El Corte Inglés, Mercadona, Lidl, Carrefour and the like stay open straight through it, and so do the restaurants and the museums.

fichasCulturais.sinal: Half seven, the square is full, and every person in it is sitting at a table with one small drink that has clearly been there a long while.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: They must have to keep buying, so if I sit down with one coffee for an hour somebody will come and move me along.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: The chair is bought once. One order holds the table and the hour after it is what the order was for — the same square empties and fills three times between six and midnight, and nobody is counted out of it.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Take a table, order one thing, and then stop ordering. Sit through the whole of it.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You get the best hour of the day for the price of one small beer, and you are sitting where the town actually is instead of where it is sold.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not at a table on a station concourse or an airport gate, where the chairs turn over on a timetable and somebody is genuinely waiting for yours.

fichasCulturais.sinal: You walk two streets with a can in your hand in one town and nothing at all happens; in the next one an officer changes direction and comes at you with a card machine in his hand.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: One of those two places is being unreasonable, because I did not do anything different in either of them.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: Almost none of this is written nationally. The street rules are set by each town hall, so the same act carries an amount in one place and passes unremarked forty kilometres inland — and since February 2026 Barcelona takes that amount from a non-resident where he is standing.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Look at what the people around you are doing with theirs: the can goes on the terrace table, and the shirt goes on at the edge of the sand rather than at the hotel door.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You spend the afternoon in exactly the places they spend it, and the money stays where it was.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not in a village inland with one bar and no seafront, where nobody has written any of it down and the shirt is nobody's business at all.

fichasCulturais.sinal: The street you walked down yesterday is closed off, there is a band on a flatbed and a crowd four deep, and nobody at either end is selling anything or checking anyone.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: This is somebody's private do and I have walked into the middle of it.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: A street closed for the town's own week is public in the plainest sense there is: the door is the end of the street, standing in it is the whole of the participation, and being looked at by people who do not know you is part of what it is for.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Stand at the edge, on your feet, and stay for the whole of it. Ask before you put a phone in anybody's face.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You get the one afternoon of the year the town puts on for itself, from inside the crowd rather than from a window.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not a procession where the crowd has gone quiet and stopped moving — there you stop too, and the phone stays down until it has gone past.

aprofundar.titulo: Who writes the rule, and the three questions that get you through an afternoon (optional reading)

secoes.titulo: Cuál, and why a two-way question beats an open one
secoes.corpo: '¿Qué me recomienda?' is the question everybody teaches and almost nobody can survive the answer to: it is open, and what comes back is a sentence at full speed with four nouns in it that you have never heard. '¿Cuál me llevo, este o aquel?' does the same social work — you are still handing the decision to the person who knows — but the answer can only be one of two things you are already looking at, and it will arrive as 'este' with a finger. That is the whole trick, and it is the same trick as '¿Hay…?' from part eight: make the reply fit in your head. Cuál is 'which one' when you are choosing between things already in view; qué is 'what' when nothing has been put in front of you yet. You will hear both and you only need one. Note that you never have to name either object: 'este' and 'aquel' — this one, that one over there — plus a finger, will do it at a cheese counter, a fishmonger's, a wine shelf and a bakery.

exemplos.pt: KWAHL meh YEH-boh — which do I take, this one or that one?
KWAHL ehs-TAH meh-KHOR oy — which is best today? (when there are more than two and you would rather she decided)

secoes.titulo: Me gusta and prefiero — the front that never moves
secoes.corpo: Both of these are learnt whole, with the thing you like hung off the end, and you never take the front of either apart. 'Me gusta' plus a thing — me gusta este barrio, me gusta el vino tinto, me gusta mucho. 'Prefiero' plus a thing or plus an action — prefiero andar, prefiero el tinto, prefiero sentarme fuera. There is an old exam question about which word in 'me gusta' is doing what, and it is genuinely of no use to you at a table: the recorded version is the version, and it has never let anybody down in a square. Two things worth knowing. First, 'me gusta mucho' is warmer than 'me gusta' and costs one word, so spend it. Second, when they ask you in the plural — '¿os gusta?' — they are asking the two of you, and the answer is still 'me gusta' or 'nos gusta' and either is fine. The neighbouring one you will hear all evening and never need to produce is '¿qué te parece?' — what do you make of it — and 'me gusta mucho' is a complete answer to that too.

exemplos.pt: preh-FYEH-roh sen-TAR-meh FWEH-rah — I'd rather sit outside
nohs GOOS-tah MOO-choh — we like it a lot (when the question came at both of you)

secoes.titulo: Se puede — the sentence with nobody in it
secoes.corpo: You will hear 'aquí no se puede' — you can't, here — more than almost anything else on this trip, on a square at midnight, at a museum door, in a chapel with a phone in your hand. It is worth recognising instantly and it is worth understanding why it sounds blunt and is not: there is no 'you' in it at all. It does not say you are not allowed; it says the thing is not done here. That is why it comes out flat and why nobody is being told off. The question form, '¿se puede beber aquí?', is the least confrontational question in the language for exactly the same reason, and if you want it, it is yours — but we have deliberately not drilled it, because '¿Puedo…?' from part six already gets you the same answer and you have already paid for it. Where 'se puede' earns its keep is on the receiving end: hear it, put the thing down or walk on, and there is nothing else to say.

exemplos.pt: ah-KEE noh seh PWEH-dheh — 👂 you can't, here. Not a telling-off; a statement about the place
seh PWEH-dheh pah-SAR — 👂 may one come through? Said at a doorway, and to nobody in particular

secoes.titulo: Who actually writes these rules, and where to look before you go
secoes.corpo: The single most useful thing in this part is not a number, it is the shape: the street rules that carry an amount are municipal ordinances, written by each ayuntamiento, and there is no national table of them. That is why the same shirtless walk is €120 to €300 in Barcelona under the civility ordinance in force since February 2026, €100 to €200 across the whole of Palma de Mallorca, and nothing at all in a village forty kilometres inland. The exceptions that are national are few and worth knowing by name: drinking in the street sits in the 2015 public security act at €100 to €600, and the taxi you take without a licence can cost the passenger up to €600 under the same sort of provision — that one comes from the UK Foreign Office's own advice for Spain. What changed in 2026, and what makes the old advice that 'they will never chase you for it' out of date, is collection: the Barcelona ordinance requires a non-resident to pay on the spot and the Guàrdia Urbana carry card readers. If you want the actual text before you travel, the search that works is the name of the town plus 'ordenanza de civismo' or 'ordenanza de convivencia' — every ayuntamiento publishes its own, in full, free.

exemplos.pt: deh KWAN-toh es lah MOOL-tah — how much is it? Ask before anything is tapped

exemplos.es: ¿Me lo puede dar por escrito, por favor?
exemplos.pt: por ehs-KREE-toh — could you give me that in writing? The receipt is your only proof you paid

secoes.titulo: The car, the sticker and the camera
secoes.corpo: The low-emission zone is the one rule in this part that is enforced without a human being anywhere near it, and it is the reason the afternoon starts with where you leave the car. Since 1 January 2026, every Spanish municipality over fifty thousand inhabitants has had to operate one, and they sit exactly where the old town is. A camera reads the plate; the penalty is a serious infraction at up to €200, halved to €100 if you pay within twenty days of the notice. The structural trap is the sticker: the DGT environmental badge is issued only to vehicles registered in Spain, so a British car does not have one and cannot simply buy one at the border — several cities run a foreign-vehicle register instead, which you complete online, city by city, before you drive in. A hire car is not automatically safe either: it carries a Spanish plate and a badge, but you still need to know which category it is in, and if a fine does arrive the hire company passes it to you with an administrative fee attached. The practical rule survives all of that unchanged: see the letters, park outside, walk in. Historic centres are small and walking them was the plan.

exemplos.pt: eh-tee-KEH-tah am-byen-TAL — does this car have an emissions badge, and which one? Asked at the hire desk, not at the barrier
seen en-TRAR — where can I park without going in?

secoes.titulo: The vape, with a date written on it
secoes.corpo: This is the most perishable thing in the whole course and it is being told to you with its date attached on purpose. As of July 2026 the position is: smoking indoors has been illegal in Spain since 2011, and smoking or vaping on a bar or restaurant terrace is still legal. On 21 July 2026 the cabinet approved a draft bill that would ban both on terraces, on beaches, at public pools, in sports grounds and national parks, would create fifteen-metre protection zones around hospitals, schools and playgrounds, and would for the first time treat an electronic cigarette, a nicotine pouch, a water pipe and heated tobacco exactly like a cigarette, whether or not there is nicotine in them. It is a draft, it is in a fragmented parliament, and nobody can honestly tell you today what month it lands. So the honest instruction is the one in the audio: if you are travelling after this, ask at the bar before you light anything, and take the answer from the person who would be fined rather than from us. This entry is on the review list for every edition of the course.

exemplos.pt: seh PWEH-dheh foo-MAR — is smoking allowed here? The one question that settles it, asked of the bar
bah-peh-AR — can I vape on the terrace? Same answer, same person
